title: Does Your Accountant Actually Cover Payroll? A Growth-Stage FAQ

body_markdown:
Between 10 and 250 employees, most companies have a CPA relationship that predates their first real payroll complexity, and nobody has gone back to write down exactly where the accountant's job ends and where payroll execution begins. That gap is rarely visible until an agency notice, a missed deposit, or a new-state hire exposes it. The questions below answer what growth-stage owners and finance leaders actually ask when they start mapping that boundary.


## Frequently asked questions


### Does my accountant handle payroll processing, or only taxes and financial statements?


Most CPA engagement letters are scoped around tax preparation, financial statement review, and advisory work, not the week-to-week mechanics of running payroll. That means calculating each pay run, depositing withheld taxes on the IRS-required schedule, and filing quarterly Form 941 returns ([IRS.gov, "About Form 941"](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-941) ) often sit outside what your CPA actually does, even if they prepare your year-end payroll tax filings. A companion piece on this site,[who handles payroll, HR, or finance at growth-stage companies](https://www.asuresoftware.com/who-handles-payroll-hr-or-finance-answers-for-growth-stage-companies/) , breaks down how these responsibilities typically get divided as headcount grows. The only reliable way to know is to ask your accountant directly which tasks are inside their scope of work.


### What payroll tasks do most CPAs not handle?


The most common gaps are the recurring, deadline-driven mechanics of running payroll rather than the analysis around it: processing each pay cycle, depositing withheld income tax and FICA on the IRS-required schedule, calculating and remitting federal unemployment tax (FUTA is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages, though most employers qualify for a credit that lowers the effective rate, per[IRS.gov, "Federal Unemployment Tax"](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/federal-unemployment-tax) ), and registering for withholding and unemployment accounts in every new state you hire into. Most CPA engagements also stop short of agency-notice response, garnishment administration, and new-hire reporting. None of these are unusual tasks for a CPA firm to exclude; they are simply outside the scope most accounting practices are staffed to run.


### Is it normal for a CPA to exclude payroll tax filings from their services?


Yes. It is common, particularly at smaller or solo CPA practices, for the engagement to cover income tax preparation and financial statement review while explicitly excluding the ongoing filing of payroll tax returns and deposits. This matters because personal liability for unremitted payroll taxes does not automatically follow the CPA; it follows whoever has authority over the remittance of withheld funds and willfully fails to remit them, which the IRS can pursue as the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty under IRC 6672 ([IRS.gov, "Trust Fund Recovery Penalty"](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/trust-fund-recovery-penalty) ). If your engagement letter is silent on who files quarterly returns, assume the answer is nobody until you confirm otherwise.


### What is the risk of assuming my accountant covers something they do not?


The risk is a compliance gap with no accountable owner: you assume the CPA is handling quarterly deposits or multi-state registration, the CPA assumes you have a payroll system handling it, and the gap only surfaces when an agency notice or penalty arrives. Under IRC 6672, the IRS can hold whoever controls remittance of withheld payroll taxes, and willfully fails to remit them, personally liable through the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty ([IRS.gov, "Trust Fund Recovery Penalty"](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/trust-fund-recovery-penalty) ), regardless of whether a CPA was involved at all. That personal exposure is exactly why confirming coverage in writing, rather than assuming it, is the cheapest fix available to you.


### When should I bring in a payroll provider alongside my accountant?


Common trigger points are hiring your first employee in a new state, crossing a headcount where manual or spreadsheet-based processing starts producing errors, receiving your first agency notice, or adding complexity like garnishments and multiple pay schedules. At that point, a platform like AsureCentral lets your team keep running payroll in-house on one connected system that includes payroll and payroll tax processing, while a managed option like AsureWorks hands the actual processing and filing to Asure specialists while you remain the employer of record. Your accountant keeps doing tax strategy and financial reporting either way; the shift is only in who executes the recurring payroll mechanics.


### Can I keep my accountant and still automate payroll processing?


Yes, and this is the normal model rather than an unusual one. Most growth-stage companies keep their CPA for tax strategy, entity structure, and financial statement work while moving the recurring mechanics of payroll onto a dedicated platform or managed service. Whether that means self-service processing on AsureCentral or handing routine payroll and HR administration to AsureWorks specialists, the CPA relationship does not have to change; only the tooling and execution around it does.


### How do I raise this with my accountant without it feeling adversarial?


Frame the conversation as clarifying a division of labor, not evaluating their performance. Ask directly which payroll tasks are included in your engagement letter, which are excluded, and who is accountable for quarterly filings and agency correspondence when something goes wrong. A guide on how to assess your accountant's actual payroll scope walks through the specific questions to bring to that conversation, and most CPAs welcome the clarity, since a documented boundary protects them from liability exposure too.


### What does a hybrid accountant-plus-platform setup actually look like day to day?


In practice, your CPA continues to own tax strategy, entity-level planning, and year-end financial statements, while a payroll platform or managed service owns the recurring cycle: calculating each pay run, depositing withheld taxes, filing quarterly returns, and keeping employee records current. A company running AsureCentral in-house still sends its CPA the reports needed for tax planning and audits, just generated from one connected system instead of a spreadsheet reconciled by hand each quarter. Two frameworks published alongside this FAQ, one mapping where a CPA's scope typically ends and one outlining how to structure the handoff itself, go into more detail on sequencing that transition.


### Who is legally responsible if a payroll tax deposit is missed, my company or my accountant?


Under IRC 6672, the IRS can assess the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty against whoever it determines had the authority to direct the remittance of withheld payroll taxes and willfully failed to do so ([IRS.gov, "Trust Fund Recovery Penalty"](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/trust-fund-recovery-penalty) ). That is typically an owner, officer, or controller inside the company rather than an outside CPA firm that was never given authority over remittance in the first place. This is exactly why written scope matters: an accountant who reviews your books quarterly is not automatically the party responsible for making sure a deposit went out on time.


### How do I know my company has outgrown what my accountant can cover?


Watch for a few concrete signals: you are hiring across new states faster than you can track registration requirements, your CPA is telling you a filing question is outside their scope, payroll errors are turning into employee trust problems, or an owner or finance leader is spending hours each pay cycle just keeping the process from breaking. A resource on[choosing the right payroll and HR service model as your company grows](https://www.asuresoftware.com/how-to-choose-the-right-payroll-and-hr-service-model-as-your-company-grows/) breaks down how to evaluate the options once you hit that point. Companies in the 10 to 250 employee range typically have a real choice between AsureCentral, for teams that want to keep ownership of execution on a connected system, and AsureWorks, for teams that want Asure specialists to run payroll and HR administration while staying the employer of record.


## The bottom line


Your accountant remains valuable for tax strategy, entity planning, and financial statements. The question this FAQ answers is where that role stops and recurring payroll execution starts, and closing that gap in writing is the fastest way to remove the risk of an unowned task. If your team is ready to make that boundary permanent, compare running payroll yourselves on AsureCentral against handing routine processing and filing to AsureWorks specialists. Both keep you as the employer of record, and both are built to work alongside the CPA relationship you already have.
